stories.title: Belfast court dismisses challenge against Drumcree parade
stories.summary: Belfast High Court has dismissed a challenge against an Orange Order parade on Portadown's Garvaghy Road this morning. It means 35 Orangemen were permitted to walk the contested route from 8am. However, the march has been delayed as the PSNI has not cleared them to march down the Garvaghy Road. This morning, thousands of people gathered at the lower end of the Garvaghy Road, blocking the road in anticipation of the march. Two cars were also parked across the road. Meanwhile, the 35 members of the Portadown District Orange Order had gathered outside the church in Drumcree just before 8am and were ready to depart. However, they said that police had been unable to clear the road for them to march and they moved back inside the church to await clearance. It is not clear at this stage how long the parade will be delayed for. The protesters were due to depart at 8am and finish no later than 9.30am.

stories.title: Court allows appeal against injunction of Drumcree parade
stories.summary: The Court of Appeal in Belfast has allowed an appeal against an injunction banning Portadown Orangemen from the nationalist Garvaghy Road tomorrow. The Lady Chief Justice, Siobhan Keegan said the high court judge who granted the injunction had "erred in law". It makes it more likely the parade will now go ahead tomorrow. However, all parties are seeking further clarity on the implications of the ruling and other further steps that may be considered. Earlier, a high court judge issued a temporary injunction stopping the parade of 35 members of the Orange Order along Portadown’s predominately nationalist Garvaghy Road. The Orange Order member who was a party to that case immediately lodged an appeal to that decision.

stories.title: Govt to give excise cut 'certainty for winter' - Harris
stories.summary: Tánaiste and Minister for Finance Simon Harris has said the Government will provide certainty around excise cuts on petrol and diesel for the winter. The Government is poised to extend the cuts until late February or early March in next month's Budget. The reductions, which were first introduced in April, were set to be unwound from the beginning of November. Speaking in the Dáil during Leaders' Questions, Mr Harris said: "Certainty for the winter period on excise is something that we can do and something that we will do." Mr Harris also pointed towards a potential cut on the carbon tax on home heating oil. He told the Dáil how he was "looking at the issue of carbon taxation in terms of how it applies to certain products" and that he was "particularly concerned around the home heating situation and the gas situation".

stories.title: CCPC searches solar panel firms over possible bid-rigging
stories.summary: A number of so-called dawn raids have been carried out by the Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (CCPC) of businesses active in the solar panel industry. CCPC officers, together with garda detective units and local gardaí, carried out the unannounced searches - which are part of an investigation into suspected bid-rigging in relation to public tenders. The consumer watchdog has the power to carry out such searches for information and evidence where it has reason to suspect that companies or individuals are not compliant with competition law. According to the CCPC, bid-rigging is a serious form of cartel conduct that occurs when businesses agree in advance how they will respond to a tender process, rather than competing independently. Such conduct may include agreeing who will win a contract, submitting cover bids, taking turns winning contracts, or agreeing not to bid. Such activity can lead to higher prices and poorer value for purchasers.

stories.title: CNN reporters blocked from Trump Air Force One trip
stories.summary: CNN reporters have been blocked from travelling with US President Donald Trump on Air Force One, in a new move by the White House to limit the news network's access. The US president last week sought to ban US news outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House, accusing them of providing only negative coverage on him. After journalists with the three outlets were blocked from entering the White House complex, a judge ordered their access to be temporarily restored, saying Mr Trump's move was likely unconstitutional. CNN was scheduled to be the TV network in the press 'pool' travelling with President Trump for a trip to Tennessee today. However, a schedule released by the White House yesterday evening did not list CNN or any of the TV networks in the TV pool rotation. The pool is a rotating group of journalists that travels with the president and provides coverage to other outlets, due to limited space.

stories.title: Dunne listed as third goalkeeper following Bazunu exit
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland defender Jimmy Dunne has been listed as Ireland's third registered goalkeeper for Sunday's Nations League clash with Israel, following Gavin Bazunu's departure from the group, according to the official UEFA website. The QPR clubman is listed wearing the number 23 shirt and as one of three listed goalkeepers in the squad, alongside Caoimhín Kelleher and Max O'Leary. The 28-year-old missed the defeat to Kosovo, but will now be included in the matchday squad, as UEFA regulations requires three registered goalkeepers in the official squad. On Saturday, Southampton's Gavin Bazunu stepped away from the team in Debrecen, following a long day of talks and votes on whether or not the game should go ahead as planned. In an official statement released later that evening, the Dubliner said he wishes his team well but would be stepping aside. "I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff and the Irish people", he said.

stories.title: Spillane eyeing quck return to the senior ranks with Tipp
stories.summary: Despite the disappointment of suffering relegation from the TG4 All-Ireland Senior Football Championship this year, Lucy Spillane is confident Tipperary can achieve an automatic return to the top-tier of ladies football in 2027. "We’ll try our best, we’re well capable of getting back up senior and performing at that level. We’ll just have to do it in intermediate now next year and then push on again." stories.title: Abankwah backed for 'great future' despite 'tough shift'
stories.summary: Heimir Hallgrimsson has backed James Abankwah to have a bright future at international level but acknowledged that the Udinese defender had a "tough shift" on Thursday night in the Republic of Ireland's disappointing UEFA Nations League group defeat to Kosovo. The Boys in Green manager opted to hand the former St Patrick's Athletic defender his first competitive start in his fifth cap. A natural centre-back, who can also fill in at right-back, the 22-year-old was given the responsibility of playing wing-back on the right of a reconstituted back five. That selection call was thrown into sharper relief at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium in Pristina because the Irish right hand side was closest to the press box in the first half. While Abankwah, in his somewhat unfamiliar role, did provide width and got forward at times, it was very apparent that Kosovo targeted that side of the pitch with regularity when they were on the attack and got some joy from those forays. Hallgrimsson conceded as much in his post-match press conference. Admitting that Chiedozie Ogbene was one of the many players to have an "off day" from his right-sided role ahead of Abankwah, the Ireland manager said: "We were open on our right side so (Kosovo) got crosses in from there."

stories.summary: Ireland scrum-half Aoibheann Reilly says there is no sense of panic in the team after last week's second-half collapse against the USA in Tallaght. Scott Bemand's side threw away a 19-point lead in the final 30 minutes as they fell to a 40-36 defeat in their opening games of the new WXV Global Series. They will have a chance to make amends on Sunday when they host Japan in Galway, the first of two games in six days against the Sakura XV. "We're looking for a full 80-minute performance this weekend," the scrum-half said. "Definitely fixes in our 'D' and just keep firing our attack because we know the Japanese have a very good defensive line as well. They're very organised, so it'll be a good challenge." And Reilly insists this weekend will be a case of minor tweaks, rather than a radical response.

stories.title: Fair City villain plays a good guy in Tall Tales & Murder
stories.summary: Full of gags, guns, and gold, and not the type of series to watch with nana, Tall Tales & Murder sees worn-out retirement home nurse Bridget (Ella Lily Hyland) and want-out car thief Paul (Casey Walsh) embark on the (mis)adventure of their lives. Joining them are previously comatose Dublin criminal Grinner (Aidan Gillen), Bridget's icy-yet-amorous boss, The Matron (Aisling O'Sullivan), and Bunny (Brian Doherty), a GAA-obsessed detective who valiantly tries to be Paul's guardian angel - and keep The Matron satisfied. In the kindest sense, Bunny is a world away from Fair City's JJ. "That's what you want as an actor - you don't want to be playing the same thing over and over again. You want that variety of character," smiled Doherty. "I've been very lucky over time to have done that. To have these two (Tall Tales & Murder and Fair City) at the same time is very unusual, and it's great craic." "JJ is fun to play the darkness and his manipulative nature is something else," the Waterford man continued.

stories.summary: Chunky belts, pencil skirts and enormous fur coats returned to the runway at Gucci’s Milan Fashion Week show, as Nicki Minaj, Romeo Beckham and more watched the Italian fashion house revive the ostentatious glamour of the 1980s. Minaj arrived in a capacious white fur coat, joining model Romeo Beckham, Canadian singer Shawn Mendes, a Gucci ambassador, and tennis stars Jannik Sinner and Aryna Sabalenka on the front row of the spring/summer 2027 show on Friday. Sinner, who has become something of a fashion fixture since becoming a Gucci ambassador in 2022, was seated alongside Anna Wintour, the former editor-in-chief of American Vogue. British model Rosie Huntington-Whiteley and former Victoria’s Secret Angel Candice Swanepoel were among those taking to the runway, which was transformed into a Gucci boutique for the occasion. Models walked in from what appeared to be the street, passing jewellery cabinets, clothing rails and shoe racks, while some stopped to admire themselves in full-length mirrors or adjust their sunglasses. It was an appropriate setting for a collection entitled The Store Show, which creative director Demna described as the first to present his complete personal vision for the Italian fashion house.

stories.title: Tension and toxicity after extraordinary day in Hungary
stories.summary: At the end of one of the most extraordinarily tense days in Irish football history, the Republic of Ireland will take the field in Debrecen to play Israel in the Nations League this evening. After months of protests and rancour, it appeared that an unlikely boycott could be in the offing at the eleventh hour after Ireland's Saturday morning press conference and training session were sensationally postponed. Having agreed to proceed from Pristina to Debrecen following a meeting on Friday, it emerged that one player was having grave doubts and wished to withdraw. The Irish Independent's Daniel McDonnell was the first to report that Gavin Bazunu was the player in question. This sparked a four-hour long player meeting, as the Irish media contingent decamped to the team base at the Mercure Hotel. Those who can recall Ireland's last World Cup appearance will have gotten flashbacks to Saipan and the sense of a fast-moving crisis unfolding behind closed meeting room doors, accompanied by a drip-feed of rumours relayed to the waiting media outside. Though given the tragic backdrop, this particular episode is unlikely to be the subject of a breezy tragicomic film in a couple of decades time.

stories.title: Abolishing private care in public hospitals to cost €140m
stories.summary: The HSE told the Public Accounts Committee that abolishing private practice in public hospitals will cost around €140 million this year. The HSE's Acting Chief Financial Officer Michael Lane said to understand the HSE's deficit it is important to look at "the policy change in private income". "That's a significant loss in income to us this year. Structurally, we are going to have to rebalance that and we are going to have to find a way without that income," he said. Mr Lane said it is "probably a loss of around €140 million to us this year". The committee earlier heard that the HSE incurred charges of €8.4 million for Covid vaccines in 2025 that had reached their expiry dates or were determined to no longer be clinically suitable for use, along with €1.5m for stocks of legacy and obsolete PPE. A further €6.7m was incurred by HSE in 2025 to dispose of this obsolete stock.

stories.title: Volkswagen announces global recall of almost 3m cars
stories.summary: German car giant Volkswagen has confirmed a recall of around 2.86 million vehicles worldwide over a potential steering risk, according to the German transport authority KBA. The affected models include VW's Tiguan, Touran, Golf and Caddy vehicles built between 2013 and 2024, and around 700,000 Audi models built from 2017 to 2024, the KBA said in brief statements this week. Corrosion could cause a bolt to fracture, leading to steering failure, though no such incidents have been reported, the statement said. "A corrosion problem" was discovered in quality control checks of the vehicles, a Volkswagen spokesman said. "We're now recalling the affected vehicles as a precautionary measure, and there have been no human injuries," he said, adding that drivers can continue using the vehicles until obtaining a dealer appointment for bolt replacements. Meanwhile, Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume may have got the green light from stakeholders for his turnaround plan, but he faces tough talks in Germany over job cuts and plant closures as well as fundamental questions over the automaker's US strategy.

stories.summary: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Europe of blocking efforts to resolve the conflict in Ukraine, after another round of strikes left 16 dead on both sides. "Europe is doing everything it can to thwart peace talks in which the Trump administration is interested," Mr Lavrov said in a fiery speech to the UN General Assembly. "The aims of the special military operation will be achieved, the threat to Russian security will be eliminated and peaceful life will come back. This will happen no matter the circumstances," he added, using Moscow's terminology for the conflict. stories.title: McMillan highlights 'green shoots' in spite of defeat
stories.summary: Munster head coach Clayton McMillan admits his side were worn down in the final quarter of their 26-20 defeat to Glasgow Warriors, but he believes there were still some "green shoots" in their overall performance. The province left a 20-14 lead slip with just over 20 minutes to play, as they had to settle for a losing bonus-point against a powerful Warriors team, who picked up their third consecutive win at Thomond Park. With 22 minutes to play, JJ Hanrahan's penalty kick nudged Munster six points in front after what had been a solid opening hour by McMillan's side, but their lack of depth off the bench showed down the stretch, in a game their head coach agreed "slowly" got away from them. "In the end, I think it became a game of territory and possession and generating pressure off that," McMillan said. "In the second half, definitely, they had the lion's share of that and probably took away a little bit of our legs. "But I was pretty proud. I think we made 100-odd tackles more than them. We kept bouncing up and going forward and fought right to the end. It wasn't good enough, but some green shoots there."

stories.title: McKenna writing latest chapter in eclectic sporting story
stories.summary:
In another life, Conor McKenna's focus would be on the Curragh this Saturday rather than the legendary Melbourne Cricket Ground. The MCG will welcome over 100,000 spectators for the 2026 AGL Grand Final with McKenna’s Brisbane Lions hoping for their sixth Premiership and their third on the trot as they come up against surprise packet Freemantle. Quirkily, their other three titles came in a three-in-a-row run from 2001 to 2003. The game will begin at 5.30am Irish time, a few hours before the gates at the Kildare racing venue will even open. Sporting worlds apart, but one of the two holds the heart of McKenna more than any other. The Eglish man is already one of Ireland’s greatest AFL exports and he also helped Tyrone to an unexpected Sam Maguire success in 2021 – but his first love was, is and always will be horses. His grandfather Malachy trained them, as did his father Pat. His cousin Liam McKenna is a jockey on the circuit. McKenna himself has dabbled in the ownership side, Cuban Grey and Battle Borne two in the McKenna Racing binder. When he won the AFL’s goal of the season at the Brownlow Medal awards earlier this week, he said the prizemoney might go towards another horse. He LOVES the ball on the ground 🇮🇪

stories.title: Rodri: Nobody can take away Manchester City's success
stories.summary: Rodri says nobody can take away Manchester City players' success and still believes in his former club’s innocence despite reports they have been found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules. The football world was rocked on Friday afternoon when a variety of outlets reported that the club had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by the league in February 2023. City have always strenuously denied the charges and a spokesperson said that "significant elements" of their legal case with the Premier League are still to be completed. Rodri ended his medal-laden spell at the Etihad Stadium in the summer and did not avoid the topic at a press conference on Friday evening nominally previewing Spain’s Nations League opener against England. "We have faced something similar back in 2020, we had a similar judicial process," the Barcelona midfielder said. "Different accusation but similar process. "There as well in the first instance we were found guilty, but we believed in the club and the innocence that the club maintained and in the end we ended up acquitted.

stories.title: Connacht overpowered late on by four-try Stormers
stories.summary: Stuart Lancaster's second season in charge of Connacht has started with a defeat, after the province fell to a 29-15 loss at home to the Stormers in Galway. Tries for Mack Hansen and Josh Ioane, and five points from the boot of Sam Gilbert, had the western province 15-10 ahead with just over 25 minutes left to play, but they couldn't deal with a powerful South African side, who grabbed two late tries to deny Connacht a bonus-point. The home side were sloppy in possession for much of the first half, and they fell 3-0 behind after 10 minutes when Stormers out-half Jurie Matthee knocked over a penalty, and on 20 minutes the tourists made their early dominance count when full-back Warrick Gelent latched onto a beautiful grubber from Andre Warner, with Matthee's conversion making it 10-0. The Stormers should have added more tries, but saw multiple chances go to waste, and on 34 minutes they were frustrated again when an intercept by Gilbert allowed Connacht go back on the attack. Lancaster's side had offered nothing in attack for most of the first half, but came alive in the five minutes before the break, Cathal Forde's hard carry for the line was followed up by Hansen (below), who dived in for a try which Gilbert converted. Incredibly, Connacht were in front by half time, and again Hansen was to the fore as his arcing run stretched the Stormers defence, and Ioane then crashed over the line for a 12-10 half time lead.

stories.title: Reviewed: Louise Kennedy's Stations is one of the year's best
stories.summary: There's a lot to be said for writers and artists who perfect a particular kind of narrative. Those who recognise that not every piece of storytelling has to be some convoluted exercise in experimentation or postmodern trickery. Hilary Mantel, for example, will be remembered for the way she evoked some of the most pivotal moments in European history. Seamus Heaney will be remembered for the dignity and complexity with which he imbued Irish rural life. Sally Rooney will be remembered for her scalpel-like dissections of post-Celtic Tiger Irish society. And Louise Kennedy, I dare say, will be remembered for her stories about lovers who are bound to one another, in spite – and sometimes because – of their irreconcilable differences. If the unfurling of the relationship at the centre of Kennedy’s new novel Stations feels familiar, then, it’s only because we are in the company of a writer who is at her most comfortable when she is pulling apart the meaty chambers of the human heart. The story follows Róisín McCaffrey and Red Camelin as they grow together, drift apart, reconcile and finally lose touch over the course of almost 30 years. "After he left she remembered the schoolbook Mags had taken in, I love Red Camelin printed inside the cover. IF ** KI NG LO VE RE DC AM EL IN she spelled as she fell asleep." Kennedy’s protagonists shine here – feel real – precisely because she resists any temptation to simplify or make them palatable. With all their messy quirks and foibles intact, they read more like the vivid character studies one would expect to find in a Gay Talese profile than fictional constructs from a story about 1980s Ireland. Red is introduced as the rebellious, troubled, brilliant eldest son of an outwardly conservative (and likely abusive) family dynamic. Róisín begins the novel as a refugee of sorts; one whose father was forced to move their family south to escape the danger he encountered as a Catholic member of the Royal Ulster Constabulary (RUC).

stories.title: Swift breaks two Spotify streaming records for 2026
stories.summary: Popstar Taylor Swift has broken two Spotify records including being named the most-streamed female artist in a day for 2026 following the release of her new single and extended album. Swift, 36, released her new song, Patient Zero, on Friday which became the most-streamed song by a female artist in a single day in 2026, according to the music streamer. She also released four new tracks as part of Life of a Showgirl: The Encore, breaking the record for the most streamed-female artist in a single day this year. It marked her first new music since she married NFL star Travis Kelce at New York's Madison Square Garden in July with the singer addressing critics of their relationship in one of her new songs, Cleveland! – the city where Kelce grew up. Other songs on the album include Patient Zero, Pink Clouding and Babylon. The extended album has been met with less positive reviews from critics and received two stars from The Telegraph, The Independent and The Guardian, the latter of which said: "It’s like watching an ambitious chorus line dancer breathlessly flay herself in the spotlight to prove herself worthy of our love."

stories.title: Things to do in Dublin this weekend (September 25-27)
stories.summary: From pop-up fashion on Grafton Street to sensory-friendly screenings in Raheny, there is plenty happening in Dublin this weekend. Woven Relations pop-up is a free event that brings an array of early-career designers together under one roof in Bewley's Grafton Street from 11am-5pm on Saturday, 26 September. Among them will be Lainey Whelan's hand-printed tights brand, T-Lainey, which has been worn onstage by award-winning singer CMAT. Attendees can purchase one-of-a-kind pieces and get to know the faces and minds behind their next favourite designers, such as Conor O’Brien Studio, Casa Cor and Moroccan brand Anouri Original. Sensinema brings a screening of The Secret of Kells to St Anne's Park, Raheny, on Saturday, 26 September 2026. Located by the Red Stable Carpark, there will be pre-screening music and chats from 3pm, with the film beginning at 4pm. Get event access guide here. Running from 24 September — 11 October, 18 days of theatre will take place all around Dublin. From world premieres and major Irish productions to extraordinary international work, some of the most exciting artists making theatre today are coming to Dublin this year. The Dublin Festival of History will run from 26 September to 11 October 2026, shining a fresh perspective on history and its importance in our everyday lives. Attracting best-selling Irish and international historians to Dublin for a high-profile programme of history talks and debate each Autumn, the festival is now celebrating its 14th year. Check out the full programme of events here. On the last Thursday of every month, Dublin stays open later. Museums, galleries, shops, cafés and venues across the city push their closing time back and put on something extra – exhibitions, live music, workshops, late openings, and the odd thing you won't see coming. See the full line-up of events here.

stories.summary: A Status Yellow rain warning is in effect for Munster, Leinster and counties Cavan and Monaghan. A Status Orange rain warning for counties Carlow, Kilkenny, Wexford, Wicklow, Cork and Waterford came into effect at 6am and expired at 10am. The separate Status Yellow rain warning came into effect at 4am and will be in place until 11am. Met Éireann has forecast heavy thundery rain and blustery conditions during the period of the warnings. The forecaster has warned of localised flooding, poor visibility and difficult travelling conditions as possible impacts from the heavy rain. Wave overtopping is also possible along southern and southeastern coastlines due to the combination of spring tides, surge and strong onshore winds.

stories.title: Public library visits increased by two million nationwide
stories.summary: Visits to public libraries around Ireland have increased by two million in the last two years. New figures show that almost 16 million visits were made to Ireland's libraries in 2025, compared with nearly 14 million in 2023. There has also been a spike in borrowing from libraries, with more than 22.8 million items issued last year. The new figures come as National Public Libraries Open Day takes place nationwide. People are being invited to visit their local library during the day to explore what they have to offer. Many will be hosting events, activities and local promotions.

stories.title: Bill seeks to bring legal rights to intersex people
stories.summary: Parents will no longer be "forced to immediately choose between male and female" on their child's birth certificate if a child is born with intersex characteristics, under a bill proposed in the Dáil today. People Before Profit-Solidarity TD Ruth Coppinger has introduced a bill to bring legal rights and recognition to non-binary and intersex people here. The bill would introduce the option of an X marker on the Gender Recognition Certificate, in addition to M (male) and F (female). The Dublin West TD says up to 10% of people are LGBTQI in surveys, and at least a third of these people identify as non-binary. She said globally around 2% of the population defines themselves this way. Deputy Coppinger said "non-binary.. refers to any person who identifies outside the binary of male and female".

stories.title: ASTI secondary teachers to take industrial action
stories.summary: Second-level teachers, who are members of the ASTI, have voted overwhelmingly in favour of taking industrial action over delays in agreeing a new public sector pay deal. ASTI members voted by 95% to 5% to take industrial action, up to and including strike action. Up to 20,000 ASTI second-level teachers will begin initial action involving withdrawal from selected activities such as the Croke Park Hours from Monday 5 October. This will be escalated to strike action, alongside other public sector unions, on 14 October. "Today's ballot result gives a clear message to the Government about the depth of feeling amongst teachers," said ASTI General Secretary Linda Kelly. "Teachers' pay has fallen significantly behind inflation. Meanwhile, the cost of living continues to climb."

stories.title: TikTok settles Alabama child safety case for $100m
stories.summary: TikTok has agreed to pay Alabama at least $100 million (€87m) and introduce limits for teen users, avoiding a trial set to begin next week in the southern US state over claims related to child safety on the platform. "Under the settlement, Alabama will receive a minimum of $100 million, due to the state within 45 days, with the potential to receive up to $300 million if certain conditions are met," the office of the Attorney General Steve Marshall said. The trial had been set to begin on Monday with jury selection. According to Mr Marshall, TikTok has agreed to introduce two-hour daily time limits and restrict access for children from midnight to 6am, among a host of other parental and safety features. Alabama's suit was the latest in a wave of litigation targeting social media companies across the United States over the harm their apps allegedly cause young users. TikTok previously settled cases that were headed for trial, including a Los Angeles lawsuit brought by a young woman and a suit from a Kentucky school district.

stories.title: Munster ground down by Glasgow for opening day defeat
stories.summary: Munster gave up a 10-point half-time lead at Thomond Park, as their BKT United Rugby Championship season started with a disappointing 26-20 defeat to Glasgow Warriors. The six-point loss brought up a sweep of defeats for the four Irish provinces, the first time that has happened on the opening weekend since 2009/10. The Scottish side ground Munster down in the final quarter, as Clayton McMillan's strength in depth was exposed. In particular, the province suffered at the scrum after the departure of new signing Kieran Brookes, who had dominated the Warriors pack on his competitive debut. Ben O'Donovan also shined for the province at scrum-half, and they were good value for their 20-14 lead when the New Zealand-born player left the game on 58 minutes, after tries for Ben O'Connor and Michael Milne, with 10 points from the boot of JJ Hanrahan. Ollie Smith and Nathan McBeth's tries had kept Glasgow in touch with Munster for the opening hour, but Franco Smith's side wore the province down with two tries in the final 15 minutes, as they defeated their bitter rivals at Thomond for the third time in a row.
